reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard haematology references
clinicalPearls: A rare inherited platelet disorder defined by absence or marked deficiency of platelet alpha-granules and their contents
The name derives from the pale, grey appearance of large agranular platelets on a Wright-stained blood film
Typically presents with mild to moderate mucocutaneous bleeding, easy bruising and menorrhagia, together with a mild macrothrombocytopenia
Most cases are caused by biallelic mutations in NBEAL2, which impair packaging of alpha-granule cargo
Because alpha-granule proteins are lost, patients often develop progressive myelofibrosis and splenomegaly over time
Serum vitamin B12 and other markers may be affected, but the diagnostic clue is the combination of grey agranular giant platelets and thrombocytopenia
Aggregation studies are variable; the key confirmatory findings are reduced alpha-granule markers and characteristic electron microscopy showing absent alpha-granules
Management principles are supportive: local haemostatic measures, antifibrinolytics, hormonal control of menorrhagia, and platelet transfusion for significant bleeding while limiting alloimmunisation
Progressive marrow fibrosis warrants long-term haematological monitoring
reference.pathophysiology: Gray platelet syndrome most often results from loss-of-function mutations in NBEAL2, a gene required for the biogenesis and cargo loading of platelet alpha-granules within megakaryocytes. Alpha-granules normally store adhesive and procoagulant proteins, growth factors and angiogenic factors that are released on platelet activation. Their absence impairs the platelet secretory response and haemostatic function, producing a bleeding tendency. Leakage of granule contents such as platelet-derived growth factor into the marrow is thought to stimulate fibroblast proliferation, explaining the characteristic progressive myelofibrosis and consequent splenomegaly and worsening thrombocytopenia seen with age.
additionalDifferentials: Bernard-Soulier syndrome and other inherited macrothrombocytopenias
additionalInvestigations: Blood film showing large pale (grey) agranular platelets
Platelet electron microscopy confirming absence of alpha-granules
Flow cytometry or assays for alpha-granule markers such as P-selectin and von Willebrand factor content
Bone marrow examination to assess for myelofibrosis
redFlags: Progressive splenomegaly with worsening thrombocytopenia from advancing myelofibrosis
Symptomatic anaemia from chronic or menstrual blood loss
Surgery or delivery without a defined haemostatic plan
reference.prognosis: Bleeding is usually mild to moderate and manageable, but the tendency to progressive myelofibrosis with splenomegaly and deepening thrombocytopenia influences long-term outlook and necessitates ongoing surveillance. Serious bleeding is uncommon but possible, particularly around surgery or trauma.
pitfalls: Mistaking the disorder for immune thrombocytopenia and giving inappropriate treatment
Overlooking the diagnosis because the agranular platelets are subtle on the film
Failing to monitor for evolving myelofibrosis
Liberal platelet transfusion leading to alloimmunisation
Neglecting iron replacement in chronic blood loss
